definition: Adamant means refusing to be persuaded or to change one's mind; unyielding.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word adamant. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know adamant should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: Dad was adamant that the tent be pitched before dark, no matter how much we wanted to swim first.
Firm is milder — a firm person holds a position calmly but can still be talked around with a good enough argument; an adamant one announces that no argument will work.
Unshakable is stronger than adamant: it rules out even the possibility of doubt, while adamant describes the emphatic refusal itself.

Insistent means demanding something firmly and over and over - an insistent person repeats the request until it is dealt with. Adamant is about refusing to be moved: someone states a position and will not be persuaded off it. You can be insistent about anything, even with no one resisting; adamant needs pressure to stand against.

Unbending means refusing to compromise - a posture that gives no ground on any point once a stance is taken. Adamant narrows to the act itself: loudly and emphatically declaring, under pressure, that one particular position will not change. Unbending describes the stiffness of the stance; adamant describes the vocal, repeated refusal to be persuaded.

Adamant means refusing to be persuaded or to change one's mind; unyielding.
The band's producer wanted to cut the seven-minute song down to radio length.
The label sent charts showing that shorter singles streamed better.
Even the drummer suggested trimming a verse.
Through every meeting, the lead singer was adamant: the song would run seven minutes or it would not be released at all.
She said it plainly, said it loudly, and never budged an inch.
The singer's loud, repeated, emphatic insistence on one specific point — the song's full length — despite pressure from every side is what makes her adamant.

When the renovation plans reached the library, every department drew up a wish list — except Mr.
Voss, who drew up a single line.
The oak card catalog would stay on the main floor.
He was adamant about it, and said so at all three planning meetings, in the same words each time.
The architects offered compromises: storage in the basement, a digital kiosk shaped like the old cabinet, a plaque.
He thanked them and repeated his sentence.
Pressure came from the board, then from the mayor's office.
Voss did not raise his voice; he simply made clear that no argument on offer was going to move him.
The finished library has glass walls, new wiring, and, on the main floor, sixty drawers of oak exactly where they have always been.
